newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Revolt imperils Australia's NSW electricity sale.
newsitem.headline: Revolt imperils Australia's NSW electricity sale.

text.p: Any privatisation of the New South Wales state electricity industry, Australia's biggest, was in doubt on Thursday after members of the Labor state government revolted over the plan.
Labor Party sources said there was probably no future for the privatisation, which state Treasurer Michael Egan proposed last month with Premier Bob Carr's backing.
"I think (the party's) caucus will insist that it go to the state conference, where I think it'll be knocked back," said one left wing Labor member of state parliament.
Egan last month circulated a discussion paper outlining a sale of the state's power stations, distributors, transmission lines and stake in the Snowy Mountains Hydroelectric Authority.
It would be the biggest privatisation in Australian history, was expected to raise up to A$22 billion and would pay off the state's debt and leave cash to spare for new public works, he argued.
But 32 Labor MPs, almost a majority of caucus, declared on Thursday that they would vote against the plan unless it was first approved by the state conference, the party's supreme policymaking body.
The opponents included six cabinet ministers and sources said more MPs were opposed to the sale but unwilling to publicly criticise Carr.
Since the caucus, a regular meeting of all Labor MPs, has to approve all of the government's legislation, sources said it now seemed unlikely that the government could gain quick approval.
More likely, caucus would insist that the issue be referred to the conference.
Right-wing unions, which sometimes back economic reforms, are generally opposed to this one.

Even if the privatisation passed through the caucus, Carr cannot get the measure through parliament without the support of the rebel MPs, because state opposition leader Peter Collins said on Thursday that his Liberal-National coalition would not help him out.
One Labor member of parliament said the unions could probably not afford to support the power sell-off because of the risk of losing members.
"They have lost a lot of membership over disaggregation."
The state government has already partially reformed its power industry through a process called disaggregation -- breaking up the collection of power stations into different business units.
Despite his Thursday promise not to help Carr, Collins has previously endorsed the privatisation and MPs expect he would pursue it if he won the election due in March 1999.
